chapter_title: Interacting with IPFS and Decentralized Storage

screens.title: Interacting with IPFS and Decentralized Storage
screens.subtitle: Use IPFS to store large, verifiable content and link it to on-chain records

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn why decentralized storage is essential when building real dApps and how IPFS provides a content-addressed, resilient place to store images, metadata, and media that would be too large or costly to store on-chain. We'll clarify what a Content Identifier, or CID, is and why immutability matters: the CID is a cryptographic hash that guarantees the retrieved file matches the stored file. You'll also see how client libraries like the ipfs-http-client and public gateways let your React dApp add and retrieve files, and how to save a small CID in a smart contract to create a verifiable link between on-chain state and off-chain content. Finally, we preview common pitfalls — pinning, availability, and privacy — so you can plan for persistence and confidentiality. By the end of the chapter you'll be ready to add files to IPFS from a React app, store CIDs in a contract, and design a simple, resilient image gallery that serves media through an IPFS gateway.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use IPFS for large or immutable off-chain content, store the CID on-chain for verifiable references, and ensure pinning to guarantee availability.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives map to practical skills you will carry into your dApp projects. First, you will be able to explain what IPFS is and why content-addressed storage matters: knowing this helps you design systems that separate verifiable references from heavy media. Second, you will learn to add and retrieve files from IPFS using tools like ipfs-http-client or public gateways; being comfortable with these APIs makes your front end resilient when serving media. Third, you will integrate IPFS into a React dApp to store immutable content for things like NFT metadata or user uploads; a concrete gallery lab helps you practice reading CIDs and displaying images through gateways. Fourth, you will link IPFS CIDs to smart contracts so that on-chain state points to off-chain content; this skill lets you keep contracts small while preserving verifiability. Each objective emphasizes a reason to care and a practical example so you can move from concept to implementation.

narration.text: These second set of objectives focuses on operational realities and design trade-offs. You will learn pinning and availability considerations so your content remains retrievable: pinning keeps a file stored on a node and prevents garbage collection, which is essential for persistent assets like NFT media. You will identify privacy and encryption requirements because IPFS content is public by default; for private data, you must encrypt before adding it and manage keys securely off-chain. screens.title: What is IPFS and content addressing?
screens.subtitle: Definition, key properties, and why it complements blockchains

narration.text: IPFS is a peer-to-peer distributed file system designed around content addressing rather than location addressing. Content addressing means you ask the network for a piece of content by its cryptographic hash, called a CID, and peers that hold that content respond. This shifts resilience and distribution to the network: the same file can be retrieved from many peers, and no single server is a required point of contact. For blockchain developers, this complements the chain because blockchains are ideal for small, verifiable state, not large media. The typical pattern is to store a small CID on-chain and the bulk data on IPFS. A concrete example: an NFT metadata JSON storing an image URL would live on IPFS; the contract stores ipfs:// followed by the CID, so anyone can verify the metadata by comparing the CID to the file contents. A common misconception is to treat IPFS as private storage — it's public by default, so sensitive data must be encrypted before adding. To check your understanding: why does storing the CID on-chain preserve verifiability while keeping on-chain costs low? That connection between CID and content integrity is the key idea to carry forward.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: IPFS is content-addressed storage; the CID ties a cryptographic hash to the file, enabling verifiable off-chain content linked from-chain.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › What is IPFS?
Content-addressed storage
Files are identified by a cryptographic hash. The CID changes if the content changes.
Why this matters
  • Immutability: a CID guarantees the exact bytes of a file.
  • Resilience: multiple peers can serve the same content.
  • Separation of concerns: blockchain stores CIDs, not large files.
Analogy
Think of a CID like a fingerprint for a file: show the fingerprint and anyone can verify the file matches it.
Common misconception
IPFS is not private by default. Public content must be encrypted off-chain if confidentiality is required.
Concrete example
An NFT metadata file uploaded to IPFS returns a CID. The smart contract stores ipfs://CID. Anyone who reads tokenURI can construct a gateway URL to fetch the metadata JSON and verify the CID matches the returned file.
Key takeaway: CIDs let you verify content integrity while keeping on-chain storage minimal and affordable.
Key Takeaway

CIDs are the cryptographic link between on-chain references and off-chain content.

screens.title: Add and retrieve files with ipfs-http-client
screens.subtitle: Code patterns for uploading and reading content from IPFS

narration.text: To add and retrieve files programmatically you commonly use the ipfs-http-client. The client talks to a running IPFS daemon or to a hosted service. The basic flow is: connect the client, call add with the file, receive a result that includes a path which is the CID, then call cat with the CID to stream the content back. In a React dApp you typically wrap these calls in async functions and handle binary data carefully. For example, after installing ipfs-http-client, you create a client instance pointing to your node or Infura. When adding, the returned result. path is your CID; store that value on-chain if you need a verifiable pointer. To retrieve, ipfs. cat yields chunks you concatenate and decode into text or blobs for images. An important distinction: gateways let browsers fetch content via HTTP using a URL like https://ipfs. io/ipfs/CID, while ipfs. cat is a direct client fetch. A frequent pitfall is assuming files stay available — without pinning, nodes might garbage collect content. Practice by writing add and cat helpers in a component and testing both local and remote nodes to see the differences in behavior.

keyIdea.title: Add & retrieve
keyIdea.text: ipfs.add returns a CID; ipfs.cat streams data back. Use client libraries for programmatic upload and gateways for browser access.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Add & retrieve files
Client code pattern
Install ipfs-http-client and create a client connected to your node or a hosted service.
import { create } from 'ipfs-http-client';

// For Infura example
const projectId = 'YOUR_INFURA_IPFS_PROJECT_ID';
const projectSecret = 'YOUR_INFURA_IPFS_PROJECT_SECRET';
const auth = 'Basic ' + Buffer.from(projectId + ':' + projectSecret).toString('base64');
const ipfs = create({
  host: 'ipfs.infura.io',
  port: 5001,
  protocol: 'https',
  headers: { authorization: auth }
});

async function addFile(file) {
  const result = await ipfs.add(file);
  return result.path; // CID
}

async function retrieve(cid) {
  const chunks = [];
  for await (const chunk of ipfs.cat(cid)) chunks.push(chunk);
  return Buffer.concat(chunks).toString('utf8');
}
Store the returned CID.path in your app or contract. When retrieving binary data like images, assemble the chunks into a blob instead of converting to utf-8 text.
Bullet summary
  • ipfs.add(file) → result.path is the CID.
  • ipfs.cat(cid) yields async iterable chunks to assemble.
  • Gateways provide HTTP access when you cannot run an IPFS client in the browser.
Example scenario
Upload a JSON metadata file for an NFT, capture its CID, and store ipfs://CID in the contract so marketplaces and wallets can fetch and verify it.
Key Takeaway

Use ipfs-http-client for programmatic upload and ipfs.cat for retrieval; gateways are the browser fallback.

screens.title: IPFS Gateways and browser access
screens.subtitle: How gateways make IPFS content reachable via HTTP

narration.text: An IPFS gateway is a bridge that lets standard web browsers request IPFS content over HTTP. The gateway receives a request like https://ipfs. io/ipfs/CID, fetches the content from the IPFS network, and serves it over plain HTTP. Gateways are useful because browsers cannot directly resolve CIDs without a client or extension. Using a gateway is simple and convenient for displaying images and metadata in a dApp, but you should be aware that public gateways are third-party HTTP servers that may impose rate limits or availability constraints. For critical production content, run your own gateway or pin content using a reliable pinning service so the gateway can fetch the data quickly from any node that stores it. A common mistake is assuming a public gateway is a durability guarantee—it's not. Gateways only proxy content; persistence still depends on nodes pinning and serving the CID. When building a gallery, construct image src using the gateway URL and consider fallback strategies if a gateway is slow or unresponsive. IPFS Gateways and browser access means gateways allow http access to ipfs content but do not themselves guarantee long-term persistence; pinning and node availability are still required.. In practical terms, how gateways make ipfs content reachable via http. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gateway purpose
keyIdea.text: Gateways allow HTTP access to IPFS content but do not themselves guarantee long-term persistence; pinning and node availability are still required.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › IPFS Gateways
Gateways provide HTTP access
Request ipfs://CIDs through a gateway URL like https://ipfs.io/ipfs/CID to receive content in a browser.
Notes
  • Gateways are convenience proxies, not persistence guarantees.
  • Run your own gateway for production to reduce external dependency.
  • Use gateway URLs in image tags to present IPFS-hosted media in dApps.
Concrete example
If tokenURI returns ipfs://Qm... you can display the image using https://ipfs.io/ipfs/Qm... in an img src attribute, or your own gateway URL.
Misconception to avoid: assuming public gateway uptime equals data persistence. Gateways fetch and serve content, but only nodes pinning the CID make the data persist long-term.
Key Takeaway

Use gateways for browser access but ensure pinning and multi-node availability for durability.

screens.title: Pinning and availability
screens.subtitle: Why pinning keeps IPFS content alive

narration.text: Pinning is the act of instructing an IPFS node to retain a piece of content and prevent it from being garbage collected. When you add content to IPFS from a client, it may be held in cache by various nodes temporarily. If you need guaranteed availability, at least one node must pin the content indefinitely. Pinning services like Pinata or hosted offerings can pin for you, or you can run your own IPFS daemon and pin there. Consider a gallery of user images: if each image is only cached and not pinned, they risk disappearing when caches are cleared. The practical workflow is: upload to IPFS, obtain the CID, pin that CID on one or more reliable nodes, then store the CID on-chain. A key misconception is that “adding” equals permanent storage; in fact, without pinning your content can be garbage collected. Finally, for mission-critical assets, pin across multiple nodes or use a service to ensure redundancy and faster retrieval through gateways. Pinning and availability means pin content on reliable nodes or services to prevent garbage collection and maintain availability for retrieval and gateway serving.. In practical terms, why pinning keeps ipfs content alive. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pinning
keyIdea.text: Pin content on reliable nodes or services to prevent garbage collection and maintain availability for retrieval and gateway serving.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Pinning & Availability
Pinning prevents garbage collection
Pinning tells a node to keep the data forever. Without pinning, data may be deleted when space is reclaimed.
Best practices:
  • Pin critical content on multiple nodes for redundancy.
  • Use trusted pinning services or run your own pinning node.
  • Combine pinning with gateway choice to improve delivery.
Failure scenario
If only one temporary node caches a file and no node pins it, the file can become unavailable when those caches expire. The remedy is explicit pinning.
Concrete action: after ipfs.add returns a CID, request pinning from your hosting provider or call ipfs.pin.add on your node. Then store the CID on-chain or in your app registry for discovery.
Key Takeaway

Pinning is essential for persistence; plan pinning into production workflows to avoid data loss.

screens.title: Privacy and mutable data patterns
screens.subtitle: Public-by-default storage and strategies for updates

narration.text: IPFS content is public by default; anyone with a CID can request the file. Therefore, do not store unencrypted sensitive data on IPFS. If you need privacy, encrypt the content before adding it and manage encryption keys outside IPFS. For mutable data, IPFS is inherently immutable because CIDs change when content changes. Practical patterns for mutation include publishing a new file and storing the new CID as the latest pointer in a smart contract, which also preserves history. Another option mentioned in the chapter is IPNS for mutable pointers, but IPNS is more complex to manage. A useful example: a user profile that changes over time can be stored as versioned JSON files on IPFS; each update produces a new CID and you update the contract's stored CID to reference the latest version. A common misconception is to expect IPFS to behave like a database — it does not. Treat IPFS as immutable storage with simple versioning or pointer strategies for mutability, combined with encryption when privacy is required. Privacy and mutable data patterns means encrypt sensitive data before adding; handle updates by publishing new cids and storing the latest cid on-chain or use mutable pointer systems with care.. In practical terms, public-by-default storage and strategies for updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Privacy & mutation
keyIdea.text: Encrypt sensitive data before adding; handle updates by publishing new CIDs and storing the latest CID on-chain or use mutable pointer systems with care.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Privacy & Mutation
Privacy: encrypt before adding
IPFS exposes content to anyone who has the CID. Encrypt off-chain for private data and manage keys securely.
Practical checklist:
  • Encrypt private files before ipfs.add.
  • Store decryption keys in a secure key manager off-chain.
  • Consider access proxies that decrypt content only for authorized users.
Mutable data patterns
Publish new CIDs for each version and update the stored CID in your contract to point to the latest version; this preserves history and keeps on-chain state small.
Example
A user updates their profile → upload new JSON → get new CID → update contract tokenURI or a registry to reference the new CID.
Key Takeaway

IPFS is immutable; handle mutation by versioning CIDs or using pointer systems and encrypt sensitive content before adding.

screens.title: Linking CIDs to smart contracts
screens.subtitle: Store a small ipfs://CID in contract state to reference off-chain content

narration.text: A common pattern is to store the CID or an ipfs:// URI on-chain so the contract holds a compact, verifiable reference to off-chain content. For example, an NFT contract can expose tokenURI that returns ipfs://Qm... where the CID points to the token's JSON metadata. The smart contract only stores a small string, which keeps gas costs manageable. When designing this flow, ensure the dApp knows how to parse the ipfs:// prefix, extract the CID, and build a gateway URL when presenting the content in a browser. Concretely, after calling ipfs. add in your frontend and receiving the CID, call a contract method such as setTokenURI with the ipfs://CID string. When reading back, replace 'ipfs://' with a gateway base to fetch images or JSON. Be careful with mutable metadata: if metadata changes, you will store the new CID and archive the old one if you need history. A frequent misconception is that storing a gateway URL on-chain is superior; it couples your contract to a third-party URL. Storing the bare CID preserves decentralization. Linking CIDs to smart contracts means store ipfs://cids in contracts to maintain verifiable, compact references to off-chain content while avoiding coupling to gateway urls.. In practical terms, store a small ipfs://cid in contract state to reference off-chain content. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: On-chain pointers
keyIdea.text: Store ipfs://CIDs in contracts to maintain verifiable, compact references to off-chain content while avoiding coupling to gateway URLs.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › CIDs in Contracts
Smart contract pointer pattern
Store ipfs://CID strings in contract variables or tokenURI so on-chain records reference immutable off-chain files.
Solidity example snippet
string public tokenURI;

function setTokenURI(string memory _tokenURI) public onlyOwner {
  tokenURI = _tokenURI;
}
Frontend flow
  1. Upload file via ipfs.add → get CID.
  2. Call contract.setTokenURI(`ipfs://${cid}`) in a transaction.
  3. Later, read tokenURI, extract the CID, and fetch via gateway.
Why store CID not gateway URL
A bare CID keeps the reference decentralized and avoids locking your dApp to a particular gateway provider.
Key Takeaway

Store ipfs://CIDs on-chain and construct gateway URLs in the frontend to display content without coupling contracts to URLs.

screens.title: React: ipfs-http-client integration patterns
screens.subtitle: File input, upload, CID capture, and status handling

narration.text: Integrating IPFS into a React dApp follows a simple pattern: initialize an ipfs-http-client instance, provide a file input to read the user's file, call ipfs. add and capture the returned CID, then send a transaction to store the CID in your contract. In practice you must handle binary blobs, connection errors, and the asynchronous nature of both IPFS and web3 transactions. The starter ImageUploader component in this chapter demonstrates state variables for web3, accounts, contract instance, selected file, uploaded CID, gallery images, and status messages. Use FileReader to read the file, pass the raw file to ipfs. add, and use the result. path as the CID. After storing the CID on-chain, refresh gallery images by calling getImages on the contract. A common pitfall is not handling user rejection of the wallet connection or ignoring upload errors; always show a clear status message. When displaying images, construct the src using a gateway URL and handle onError fallback gracefully. These patterns help create a robust upload-and-display flow in React. React: ipfs-http-client integration patterns means initialize ipfs client, capture file, ipfs.add to get cid, store cid on-chain, fetch cids to render gallery via gateways with error handling.. In practical terms, file input, upload, cid capture, and status handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: React integration
keyIdea.text: Initialize ipfs client, capture file, ipfs.add to get CID, store CID on-chain, fetch CIDs to render gallery via gateways with error handling.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › React Integration
Uploader pattern
Keep state for file, CID, gallery, and status; handle async flows for both IPFS and smart contract calls.
// Example flow (conceptual)
const file = selectedFile;
const result = await ipfs.add(file);
const cid = result.path; // store CID on-chain
await contract.methods.uploadImage(cid).send({ from: accounts[0] });
// fetch images
const cids = await contract.methods.getImages().call();
Show progress messages: connecting to MetaMask, uploading to IPFS, storing CID on-chain, and refreshing gallery. Also clear file inputs after success to avoid accidental re-uploads.
Error handling & UX
  • Show descriptive messages when MetaMask access is denied.
  • Catch ipfs.add errors and surface them to the user.
  • Gracefully handle broken gateway images with fallback placeholders.
Example UI behavior
After upload, display the returned CID and update the gallery by fetching all CIDs from the contract.
Key Takeaway

Design for async flows and failures: IPFS upload, on-chain transaction, and gateway retrieval are all asynchronous and can fail separately.

screens.title: Hands-on: Decentralized Image Gallery steps
screens.subtitle: Step sequence to build the ImageGallery dApp from the chapter activity

narration.text: The Image Gallery lab in this chapter is a practical sequence you can follow. First, deploy the ImageGallery Solidity contract that stores an array of string CIDs and exposes uploadImage and getImages methods. Next, set up a React component with Web3 and ipfs-http-client; ensure MetaMask or another wallet is available. Third, implement a file input handler that reads the chosen image, calls ipfs. add to upload, captures result. path as the CID, then sends a transaction to uploadImage on the contract. Fourth, implement a fetch routine that calls getImages and renders each CID as an image by constructing a gateway URL. Finally, add operational polish: show connection status, handle upload errors, display CID and transaction receipts, and add pinning via a service for production content. A key misconception is to assume the gallery will always show images right away; in reality, IPFS propagation and gateway caching can introduce delays, so build UI feedback and retries into the gallery. screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Pinning, availability, and error handling patterns

narration.text: When working with IPFS, several recurring mistakes cause frustration. First, not pinning content leads to eventual unavailability; adding without pinning is transient. Second, assuming a public gateway equals durability is false: gateways only proxy whatever nodes have the content, and if no node has pinned it, the file may not be served. Third, neglecting error handling for both IPFS uploads and web3 transactions leaves users in the dark when something fails. To troubleshoot, verify the CID returned by ipfs. add, check pin status on your node or service, and query the contract to confirm the CID was stored. For images that do not load, attempt fetching the gateway URL directly to see whether the gateway can retrieve the content. Use status messages and retries in the UI, and log transaction receipts to confirm on-chain storage. Another helpful step is pinning the CID on multiple nodes or via a pinning service to improve availability. These patterns help you move from a fragile prototype to a production-ready experience. Common mistakes and troubleshooting means verify cid output, pin critical content, handle upload and transaction errors, and test gateway retrieval to diagnose availability issues.. In practical terms, pinning, availability, and error handling patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Verify CID output, pin critical content, handle upload and transaction errors, and test gateway retrieval to diagnose availability issues.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Troubleshooting
Common mistakes
  • Not pinning content and expecting permanence.
  • Storing gateway URLs on-chain and creating coupling to a provider.
  • Not handling IPFS or transaction errors in the UI.
Quick checks
Confirm the CID returned by ipfs.add, query your contract to verify storage, and test gateway fetches for the CID.
Remediation steps
  1. Pin the CID on at least one reliable node or via a pinning service.
  2. Implement clear UI status messages and retries for uploads and fetches.
  3. Prefer storing the bare CID on-chain rather than a gateway URL.
These practices reduce user frustration and harden the integration between your dApp, IPFS, and the blockchain.
Key Takeaway

Treat pinning and error handling as first-class parts of your IPFS integration to maintain availability and trust.

screens.title: Design checklist and best practices
screens.subtitle: Guidelines for production-ready IPFS usage in dApps

narration.text: Before shipping an IPFS-enabled dApp, validate a concise checklist. First, confirm your upload flow returns a valid CID and that you handle errors and retries. Second, ensure pinning: pin critical files using a trusted service or multiple nodes to guarantee availability. Third, store only the CID or ipfs://CID in contracts to avoid locking the contract to a gateway. Fourth, encrypt any sensitive data before adding to IPFS and manage keys off-chain. Fifth, provide robust frontend UX: clear connection prompts, upload progress, transaction receipts, and image fallbacks when gateways are slow. Sixth, test both local IPFS daemon behavior and remote hosted services because timing and propagation differ. Finally, document how you will rotate or update content: a versioning strategy based on new CIDs preserves history while keeping the current pointer on-chain. narration.text: Let's walk a concrete example used in the chapter: an NFT metadata flow. The user selects an image in your React UI. The app uploads the file to IPFS using ipfs-http-client and receives a CID. Next, the frontend calls a contract method such as setTokenURI with ipfs://CID; the contract stores this string in a small state variable. Later, a marketplace or wallet reads tokenURI, extracts the CID, and constructs a gateway URL like https://ipfs. io/ipfs/CID to fetch the JSON and image. This pattern keeps on-chain storage tiny, preserves verifiability because the CID is cryptographic, and enables rich media without bloating gas costs. Watch for pitfalls: pin the image to avoid timeouts, encrypt if the asset is private, and avoid storing gateway URLs on-chain to maintain decentralization. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's consolidate the essential concepts you should retain. First, IPFS is content-addressed: files are fetched by hash and identified by CIDs. Second, CIDs are immutable and verifiable, so storing a CID on-chain gives you a trustable pointer to off-chain content. Third, ipfs-http-client is a common tool to add and retrieve files programmatically, and gateways allow browsers to fetch IPFS content via HTTP. Fourth, pinning is required to guarantee persistence; without pinning, content can be garbage collected. Fifth, privacy requires encryption before adding, because IPFS content is public by default. Keep these points in mind as design constraints and opportunities when building decentralized applications that serve large media without inflating on-chain state. screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for daily development

narration.text: Keep these three short reminders handy while building: one, always treat IPFS as content-addressed storage — CIDs change when content changes. Two, pin important content on reliable nodes or services to guarantee availability; adding alone is not a persistence promise. Three, store the CID on-chain rather than gateway URLs to maintain decentralization and flexibility. These rules help you design dApps that combine the verifiability of blockchain with the scalability of IPFS.
